title: Redwood discovery - Reliability & multi-region fallbacks with Aerion Systems
summary: Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and multi-region fallback strategies. Aerion is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive payments workloads. Key concerns: regional failover, deterministic SLA for Dedicated, data residency, KMS/HSM integration, and cost impact of multi-region active-active. Agreed next step: run a short benchmark, share security pack & Dedicated pricing, schedule technical deep dive with infra team.
topics: Multi-region routing and active-active vs active-passive
next_steps: Jamie to send Dedicated pricing and reserved capacity options (due 2026-07-09)
Sofia to share security docs (SOC2/ISO attachments) and KMS integration notes (due 2026-07-08)
Schedule technical deep-dive with Aerion infra team (aim for week of 2026-07-13)
Set up benchmark: 1 region vs multi-region routing run with 1k synthetic QPS (SRE to provide sample payloads)
action_items: Jamie (AE) - Send Dedicated pricing + case study - 2026-07-09
Sofia (SE) - Share security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS, audit logs) - 2026-07-08
Marcus (Aerion SRE) - Share representative traffic profile and blackout window tolerance - 2026-07-10
Liam (SE) - Prep benchmark plan and infra checklist - 2026-07-12
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. This is Jamie from Redwood, AE on the account. Today Sofia and Liam are with me from engineering. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Shah: Doing well, thanks. Busy week but excited to chat through reliability stuff.
[00:12] Sofia Mendes: Hi Priya, Marcus, Nina, Ethan. We'll try to keep this focused - want to understand your production constraints and what failure modes worry you most.
[00:21] Marcus Lee: Cool. To set context: Aerion's payments fraud flows are latency sensitive - sub 120ms p95 ideally for decisions. We run in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 today, and we're aiming for multi-region resilience without doubling costs.
[00:36] Ethan Kim: Also, some of our prompts hit big context windows so KV cache behavior matters; cold-start cost is a concern.
[00:44] Liam O'Connor: Got it. Quick question on deployment preference - are you leaning Hosted, Dedicated, or Private?
[00:50] Priya: We want to evaluate all three. Hosted for speed and sandboxing; Dedicated if we need predictable throughput/SLA; Private for data residency compliance in EU. Main thing is continuous availability.
[01:02] Nina Torres: From security POV, we need KMS/HSM integration, SSO, audit logs, and proof of SOC2. We also need encryption at rest and in transit.
[01:12] Sofia: Redwood has SOC2 and we can share the pack - Dedicated and Private have more controls around KMS and private networking. We'll send docs after.
[01:20] Marcus: Great. On failover, we want automatic region-to-region routing if a region has capacity or outage issues. How does Redwood do that?
[01:28] Liam: There are a few approaches. For Hosted we support smart routing policies - you can prefer lowest-latency region but fall back to a secondary region. For Dedicated you can have reserved capacity in multiple regions and an active-active routing policy, or active-passive if you care about cost.
[01:44] Marcus: Active-active sounds ideal but worried about state/billing and KV cache coherence.
[01:50] Sofia: Right - with active-active you'd want prefix caching and sticky routing where possible. Our runtime has KV cache sharding and prefix cache that can be warmed across nodes; for consistency you can use short TTLs and sync warming through a cache replication job during failover. It's not fully automatic across clouds without some orchestration.
[02:06] Marcus: That sounds like additional engineering work. What's the fallback behavior if a model instance fails mid-request? Do you retry on a different variant?
[02:15] Liam: The platform supports automatic retry to compatible model variants - e.g., if you're on a large quantized model and capacity is constrained, Redwood can route to a smaller model variant with configurable fallback policy. Retries are bounded and can be synchronous or async depending on your SLO tolerance.
[02:30] Ethan: If we fallback to a smaller model for latency, how do we ensure quality doesn't regress for fraud detection thresholds?
[02:36] Sofia: We recommend a staged fallback policy: first try hot cache and same model + different node, then try compatible model variant (same architecture, lower precision), and if still failing, route to a simpler rule-based baseline. Also tie these fallbacks to telemetry so you can observe precision/recall drift.
[02:53] Priya: Telemetry is critical - we need token-level latency + error breakdowns per route.
[02:58] Jamie: Redwood Console provides per-route latency, token cost, and error traces. We can set alerting on error budgets too.
[03:06] Nina: On SLA - what do we offer for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[03:10] Jamie: Hosted has a best-effort uptime and our SLAs typically apply to Dedicated reserved capacity. For Dedicated we have an SLA option (e.g., 99.9x depending on tier) and guaranteed throughput. Exact numbers are in the contract but we can go over typical SLAs.
[03:25] Marcus: We need deterministic tail latency guarantees - p99 under 300ms for signature endpoints. Can Dedicated meet that?
[03:31] Liam: Yes, with reserved capacity sized for your peak concurrency and steady-state batching configuration, Dedicated can consistently hit p99 latencies under those bounds for typical transformer models. We also offer burst capacity options for spikes.
[03:43] Marcus: What about cross-region network penalties - if we route eu traffic to us-east during an outage, latency jumps a lot. Is there a preferred pattern?
[03:52] Sofia: For geo-sensitive low-latency workloads, active-active with local capacity is preferred. If that's cost-prohibitive, you can do active-passive with a short-circuiting fallback: synchronous requests prefer local region and fail fast to a queue that is processed asynchronously in another region, or use a lighter-weight sync fallback with faster but lower-quality model.
[04:12] Priya: So that's an engineering tradeoff we need to agree on: do we accept occasional higher-latency decisions vs queuing and slower processing.
[04:20] Ethan: Related to cost - how much more does multi-region Dedicated cost? Do you have ballpark?
[04:25] Jamie: Multi-region reserved capacity is effectively additive - you pay for reserved nodes per region. We provide recommendations to minimize waste via auto-scale and burst pools. We'll send ballpark numbers in the pricing doc.
[04:35] Marcus: We also have regulatory constraints for EU data residency - logs and telemetry for EU customers must not leave region. Can Redwood restrict telemetry?
[04:44] Sofia: Yes, Private and Dedicated with private control plane options support region-scoped telemetry retention and audit log routing to customer-managed S3. Hosted can be configured with regional ingress but has limitations on full data egress controls. For strict residency, Private or on-prem is recommended.
[04:59] Nina: HSM/KMS - do you support Cloud KMS and external HSMs?
[05:04] Liam: We integrate with common cloud KMS providers and customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private. For on-prem HSM we do a connector pattern; we can share integration docs.
[05:13] Priya: Good. For our POC we'd like to run a benchmark with our traffic shape, simulate region failover and measure p95/p99 and cost. What's the minimal setup for that?
[05:22] Sofia: Minimal: one reserved Dedicated pool in primary region (us-east-1) and a smaller standby pool in secondary (eu-west-1) OR run Hosted + Dedicated hybrid for the POC. We'll need your sample requests and expected concurrency. Liam can sketch out infra steps.
[05:34] Liam: I'll prepare a checklist: sample payloads, auth keys, region endpoints, expected QPS, and any SLOs you want enforced. We can run a two-run test: normal routing, then force failover by draining region and measure switchover time and latency.
[05:47] Marcus: How do you enforce canary or gradual rollouts of model versions? Because model changes can create quality regressions that look like outages.
[05:55] Sofia: Redwood supports canary routes and A/B traffic splits at the routing layer. You can pin a percentage to a new model and monitor quality via eval sets and production prompts. We also have automatic rollback policies based on error/quality thresholds you define.
[06:08] Priya: If we need guaranteed 4 nines or something extreme, is that negotiable?
[06:13] Jamie: Enterprise contracts can include tighter SLAs with financial remedies and runbooks; however, the technical guarantees rely on Dedicated architecture and agreed runbooks. For 99.99 you'd likely need multi-region active-active reserved capacity plus network redundancy and runbook commitments.
[06:28] Nina: We need a proof of SOC2 + penetration test summary to show to compliance. Can you provide redacted reports?
[06:36] Sofia: Yes - we'll send SOC2 Type II summary and the penetration test executive summary. For Private we can include the on-prem checklist.
[06:45] Ethan: A small nit: we use token caching heavily. How deterministic is KV cache eviction across nodes during failover - could we see cold-start regressions?
[06:55] Liam: Cold start is possible. We mitigate with prefix/KV cache warming, and you can warm model caches proactively via synthetic traffic or pub/sub hooks that rehydrate caches. For critical paths we recommend sticky sessions and cache pre-warming as part of the failover playbook.
[07:10] Marcus: During failover window, how long to route to fallback model? Seconds? Minutes?
[07:15] Sofia: That depends on configuration. We default to short retries (500ms backoff) and then fallback within a couple of seconds to a compatible model variant. For region-level failover, switchover policy can be immediate or you can require health checks for X seconds. We surface these settings in config.
[07:29] Priya: Any customers using Redwood for payments at scale you can reference?
[07:33] Jamie: We have a couple of finance/payments customers - we'll include anonymized case studies in the follow-up pack.
[07:40] Marcus: Let's talk incident tolerance - suppose a zone or AZ goes down in us-east - what's the expected impact?
[07:47] Liam: With Dedicated across multiple AZs you'd lose some nodes but capacity should remain if cluster sized with AZ redundancy. If you used single-AZ Dedicated you'd see capacity loss. For Hosted we automatically shift across AZs but there can be transient throttles.
[08:00] Ethan: Is there built-in request hedging to reduce variance?
[08:03] Sofia: We have request hedging features where parallel probes are sent to multiple nodes, and the fastest response is returned; it's configurable due to cost implications. Customers use it for critical paths to reduce p99 variance.
[08:15] Marcus: Costly but interesting. For our POC let's start with a Hosted + Dedicated hybrid - keep some traffic on Hosted while we test Dedicated performance.
[08:24] Jamie: Sounds good. We'll propose a POC plan that minimizes up-front Reserved commitment - short reserved pool + burst capacity and bench on Hosted baseline.
[08:32] Nina: About audit logs - do you support pushing them to our Splunk instance or S3?
[08:37] Sofia: Yes, Dedicated/Private can route audit logs to customer sinks (S3, GCS, Splunk) with region scoping. Hosted can stream logs but may have cross-region considerations.
[08:46] Priya: Any constraints on model artifacts for Private? We may want to host model weights in our VPC for compliance.
[08:53] Liam: For Private and on-prem deployments customers can host model weights on their storage. Redwood's runtime can load models from customer buckets or internal registries; we'll provide the onboarding checklist.
[09:03] Marcus: Let's agree on the measurable success criteria for the POC: p95 < 120ms in primary region, p99 < 300ms, failover switchover < 15s with no more than 1% request errors, and telemetry completeness for audit.
[09:18] Jamie: Perfect - we'll put that in the SOW for the POC.
[09:22] Priya: Timeline-wise we'd like to run the POC in the next 3 weeks. Is that feasible?
[09:27] Sofia: Yes, if we get sample payloads and a brief infra contact we can spin up a small Dedicated pool and run the tests.
[09:34] Jamie: I'll follow up with an email with next steps and the initial pricing doc.
[09:38] Marcus: Quick question - does Redwood provide prebuilt Prometheus metrics or do we have to instrument?
[09:43] Liam: We export Prometheus metrics and provide Grafana dashboards; you can pull raw metrics or integrate via our tracing hooks.
[09:49] Ethan: Good. One more: how does model warm-up cost count towards billing?
[09:54] Sofia: Warm-up runs are billable if run in Hosted, but with Dedicated warm-up on reserved nodes is considered part of capacity (so no incremental API billing), though we track token consumption. We'll include cost notes.
[10:05] Priya: Ok that's helpful. Any other risks we should know?
[10:09] Sofia: Main risks are cache cold starts during failover, and quality drift with model fallbacks - both mitigated by warming, telemetry, and staged rollouts.
[10:18] Jamie: Alright let's recap action items and next steps. Sofia will share security docs; Jamie will send pricing and case studies; Liam will prep benchmark checklist; Marcus will share traffic profile. We'll aim to schedule the technical deep-dive next week.
[10:34] Priya: Thanks all. Appreciate the clarity.
[10:36] Nina: Thanks - we'll look for the SOC2 and pen test summaries.
[10:39] Jamie: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[10:41] [call ends]
notes: Customer prioritizes latency-sensitive payments decisions across us-east and eu-west
Preferred POC approach: Hosted + small Dedicated pool for baseline and failover testing
